problems.problem: We are given $5771$ weights weighing $1,2,3,\ldots,5770,5771$. We partition the weights into $n$ sets of equal weight. What is the maximal $n$ for which this is possible?
Evaluate the sum $$\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1\cdot3}}+\sqrt{2-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{3\cdot5}}+\sqrt{3-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{5\cdot7}}+\cdots+\sqrt{40-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{79\cdot81}}.$$

In the government of some foreign country there are $12$ ministers. Each minister has $5$ friends and $6$ enemies in the government (friendship and enmity are symmetric relations). A triple of ministers is called uniform if all three of them are friends with each other, or all three of them are enemies of each other. How many uniform triples are there?

Let $\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3$ be three congruent circles that are tangent to each other. A circle $\beta$ is tangent to them at the points $A_1,A_2,A_3$, respectively. Let $P$ be a point on $\beta$ different from $A_1,A_2,A_3$. For $i=1,2,3$, let $B_i$ be the second intersection point of the line $PA_i$ with the circle $\alpha_i$. Prove that triangle $B_1B_2B_3$ is equilateral.

We have two lists of numbers: one initially contains $1,6,11,\ldots,96$, and the other initially contains $4,9,14,\ldots,99$. In every turn, we erase two numbers from one of the lists and write $\frac{1}{3}$ of their sum (not necessarily an integer) in the other list. We continue this process until no move is possible.

(a) Prove that at the end of the process there is exactly one number in each list.

(b) Prove that these two numbers are not equal.

There are $N$ red cards and $N$ blue cards. Each card has a positive integer between $1$ and $N$ (inclusive) written on it. Prove that we can choose a nonempty subset of the red cards and a nonempty subset of the blue cards such that the sum of the numbers on the chosen red cards equals the sum of the numbers on the chosen blue cards.

Consider the number $$\left(101^2-100^2\right)\cdot\left(102^2-101^2\right)\cdot\left(103^2-102^2\right)\cdots\left(200^2-199^2\right).$$ (a) Determine its units digit.

(b) Determine its tens digit.

Let $A_1A_2A_3$, $B_1B_2B_3$, $C_1C_2C_3$ be three equilateral triangles, the vertices of each triangle numbered clockwise. It is given that $A_3=B_3=C_3$. Let $M$ be the centroid of triangle $A_1B_1C_1$ and $N$ the centroid of triangle $A_2B_2C_2$. Prove that triangle $A_3MN$ is equilateral.

Let $ABCDEF$ be a convex hexagon. Inside the hexagon there is a point $K$ such that $ABCK$ and $DEFK$ are both parallelograms. Prove that the three lines joining $A,B,C$ to the midpoints of the segments $CE,DF,EA$, respectively, meet at one point.

We are given a row of $n\geq7$ tiles. On each of the leftmost $3$ tiles there is a white piece, and on each of the rightmost $3$ tiles there is a black piece. White and Black play in turns, White starting. In each move a player takes a piece of his color and moves it to an adjacent tile, provided that tile is not occupied by a piece of the same color. If the new tile is empty, nothing happens. If it is occupied by a piece of the opposite color, both pieces are destroyed. The player who destroys the last two pieces wins the game. Which player has a winning strategy, and what is it? (The answer may depend on $n$.)
Let $p$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients satisfying $p(16)=36$, $p(14)=16$, $p(5)=25$. Determine all possible values of $p(10)$.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Find the maximal real number $k$ such that for any $n$ real numbers $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ $$\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots+x_n^2}\geq k\cdot\min(|x_1-x_2|,|x_2-x_3|,\ldots,|x_{n-1}-x_n|,|x_n-x_1|).$$
Find one real value of $x$ satisfying $$\frac{x^7}{7}=1+\sqrt[7]{10}\,x\left(x^2-\sqrt[7]{10}\right)^2.$$

(a) Find an example of three positive integers $a,b,c$ satisfying $31a+30b+28c=365$.

(b) Prove that any triple $a,b,c$ of positive integers satisfying this condition also satisfies $a+b+c=12$.
The altitudes of a triangle have lengths $\frac{1}{5},\frac{1}{5},\frac{1}{8}$. Evaluate the area of the triangle.
Prove that the number $$\left(\frac{76}{\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{77}-\sqrt[3]{75}}-\sqrt[3]{5775}}+\frac{1}{\frac{76}{\sqrt[3]{77}+\sqrt[3]{75}}+\sqrt[3]{5775}}\right)^3$$ is an integer.

Let $k,m,n$ be positive integers such that $n^m$ is divisible by $m^n$ and $m^k$ is divisible by $k^m$.

(a) Prove that $n^k$ is divisible by $k^n$.

(b) Find an example of $k,m,n$ satisfying these conditions, where all three numbers are distinct and greater than $1$.

Let $ABCD$ be a tetrahedron. Denote by $S_1$ its inscribed sphere, tangent to all four faces, and by $S_2$ the exscribed sphere lying outside the face $ABC$, tangent to the face $ABC$ and to the planes of the faces $ABD$, $ACD$, $BCD$. Let $K$ be the point of tangency of $S_1$ with the face $ABC$, $L$ the point of tangency of $S_2$ with the face $ABC$, and $T$ the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to the face $ABC$. Prove that $L,T,K$ lie on one line.

Let $n\geq1$ be an integer. $n$ lamps are placed in a line. At minute $0$ some lamps are on (maybe all of them). Every minute the state of the lamps changes: a lamp is on at minute $t+1$ if and only if at minute $t$ exactly one of its neighbors is on (the two lamps at the ends have one neighbor each, all other lamps have two neighbors). For which values of $n$ can we guarantee that all lamps will be off after some time?

The Fibonacci sequence $F_n$ is defined by $F_0=0$, $F_1=1$ and $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$ for all integers $n\geq2$. Let $p\geq3$ be a prime number.

(a) Prove that $F_{p-1}+F_{p+1}-1$ is divisible by $p$.

(b) Prove that $F_{p^{k+1}-1}+F_{p^{k+1}+1}-\left(F_{p^k-1}+F_{p^k+1}\right)$ is divisible by $p^{k+1}$ for every positive integer $k$.

Nina and Meir are walking along a $3$ km path towards grandma's house. They start walking at the same time from the same point. Meir's speed is $4$ km/h and Nina's speed is $3$ km/h. Along the path there are several benches. Whenever Nina or Meir reaches a bench, they sit on it for some time and eat a cookie. Nina always takes $t$ minutes to eat a cookie, and Meir always takes $2t$ minutes, where $t$ is a positive integer. It turns out that Nina and Meir reached grandma's house at the same time. How many benches were there? Find all options.

We are given a cone with height $6$ whose base is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$. Inside the cone there is an inscribed cube: its bottom face lies on the base of the cone, and all of its top vertices lie on the cone. What is the length of the edge of the cube?

Denote by $S(n)$ the sum of the digits of $n$. Given a positive integer $N$, we consider the following process: we take the sum of digits $S(N)$, then its sum of digits $S(S(N))$, then $S(S(S(N)))$, and so on, until we are left with a one-digit number. The number of times we have to apply $S(\cdot)$ is called the depth of $N$. For example, the depth of $49$ is $2$, since $S(49)=13$ and $S(13)=4$, and the depth of $45$ is $1$, since $S(45)=9$.

(a) Prove that every positive integer $N$ has a finite depth.

(b) Let $x(n)$ be the minimal positive integer with depth $n$. Find the residue of $x(5776)$ modulo $6$.

(c) Find the residue of $x(5776)-x(5708)$ modulo $2016$.

The Fibonacci sequence $F_n$ is defined by $F_1=F_2=1$ and $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$ for all integers $n\geq3$. Let $m,n\geq1$ be integers. Find the minimal degree $d$ for which there exists a polynomial $f(x)=a_dx^d+a_{d-1}x^{d-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$ satisfying $f(k)=F_{m+k}$ for all $k=0,1,\ldots,n$.

Points $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_{12}$ are the vertices of a regular $12$-gon, in this order. The $12$ diagonals $A_1A_6,A_2A_7,A_3A_8,\ldots,A_{11}A_4,A_{12}A_5$ are marked. Let $X$ be a point of the plane, and let $B_1,B_2,\ldots,B_{12}$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $X$ to the marked diagonals, so that $B_1$ lies on $A_1A_6$, $B_2$ on $A_2A_7$, and so on. Evaluate the ratio $$\frac{XA_1+XA_2+\cdots+XA_{12}}{B_1B_6+B_2B_7+\cdots+B_{12}B_5}.$$
Find all functions $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that $$f(x(2y+1))=f(x(y+1))+f(x)f(y)$$ for all integers $x,y$.

$n$ people sit in a circle. Each of them is either a liar (always lies) or a truth-teller (always tells the truth), and everybody knows who is who. In turn, each person says: "the person two seats to my left is a truth-teller". It is known that there is at least one liar and at least one truth-teller in the circle.

(a) Is it possible that $n=2017$?

(b) Is it possible that $n=5778$?

An arithmetic sequence is an infinite sequence of the form $a_n=a_0+n\cdot d$ with $d\neq 0$. A geometric sequence is an infinite sequence of the form $b_n=b_0 \cdot q^n$ with $q\neq 1,0,-1$.

(a) Does every arithmetic sequence of integers have an infinite subsequence which is geometric?

(b) Does every arithmetic sequence of real numbers have an infinite subsequence which is geometric?
Determine the minimal and the maximal values of the expression $$\frac{|a+b|+|b+c|+|c+a|}{|a|+|b|+|c|},$$ where $a,b,c$ are real numbers.

The three-digit number $999$ has a special property: it is divisible by $27$, and its digit sum is also divisible by $27$. The four-digit number $5778$ also has this property, since it is divisible by $27$ and its digit sum is divisible by $27$. How many four-digit numbers have this property?

The sequence $a_n$ is defined for $n\geq 10$ by the following rules:

• $a_{10}=5778$;

• if $a_n=0$, then $a_{n+1}=0$;

• if $a_n\neq0$, then $a_{n+1}$ is the number whose base-$(n+1)$ representation equals the base-$n$ representation of the number $a_n -1$.

For example, $a_{11}=5\cdot11^3+7\cdot11^2+7\cdot11+7=7586$ and $a_{12}=5\cdot12^3+7\cdot12^2+7\cdot12+6=9738$.

(a) Does there exist $n\geq10$ with $a_n=0$?

(b) Is $a_{1\,000\,000}=0$?

(c) Is $a_{100^{100^{100}}}=0$?

In the corners of a triangle $ABC$ there are three circles with the same radius, each tangent to two of the sides of the triangle. The vertices of a triangle $MNK$ lie on different sides of triangle $ABC$, and each side of $MNK$ is tangent to one of the three circles. Likewise, the vertices of a triangle $PQR$ lie on different sides of triangle $ABC$, and each side of $PQR$ is tangent to one of the three circles. Prove that the triangles $MNK$ and $PQR$ have the same inradius.

A uniform covering of the integers $1,2,\ldots,n$ is a finite multiset of subsets of $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ such that each number lies in the same number of sets of the covering. A covering may contain the same subset several times, it must contain at least one subset, and it may contain the empty set. For example, $(\{1\},\{1\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\},\{2,4\})$ is a uniform covering of $1,2,3,4$ (every number occurs in two sets), and the covering consisting only of the empty set is also uniform (every number occurs in zero sets).

Given two uniform coverings, their sum (denoted by $\oplus$) is the uniform covering obtained by taking the sets of both coverings together. For example, $$(\{1\},\{1\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\},\{2,4\})\oplus(\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\})=(\{1\},\{1\},\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\},\{2,3\},\{3,4\},\{2,4\}).$$ A uniform covering is called non-composite if it is not the sum of two uniform coverings. Prove that for every $n\geq1$ there are only finitely many non-composite uniform coverings of $1,2,\ldots,n$.

Sophie wrote on a piece of paper every integer from $1$ to $1000$ (inclusive) in decimal notation.

(a) Which digit did Sophie write most often?

(b) Which digit did Sophie write least often?
Does there exist an infinite sequence of primes $p_1, p_2, p_3, \ldots$ such that $p_{n+1}=2p_n+1$ for each $n$?
Let $ABC$ be a triangle, $X$ the point where the incircle touches $BC$, and $Y$ the second intersection point of the segment $AX$ with the incircle. Prove that $$AX+AY+BC>AB+AC.$$

Danny likes seven-digit numbers with the following property: the units digit is divisible by the tens digit, the tens digit is divisible by the hundreds digit, and so on. For example, Danny likes the number $1133366$ but does not like $9999993$. Is the number of numbers Danny likes divisible by $7$?
Solve the following equation in positive numbers: $$(2a+1)(2a^2+2a+1)(2a^4+4a^3+6a^2+4a+1)=828567056280801.$$

$21$ players participated in a tennis tournament in which each pair of players played exactly once and each game had a winner (no ties). The organizers found that each player won at least $9$ games and lost at least $9$. They also found triples of players $A,B,C$ in which $A$ won against $B$, $B$ won against $C$ and $C$ won against $A$, and called such triples problematic.

(a) What is the maximum possible number of problematic triples?

(b) What is the minimum possible number of problematic triples?

A triangle $ABC$ is given. The circle $\omega$ with center $I$ is tangent to the segments $BC,AC,AB$ at $D,E,F$, respectively. Rotating $ABC$ by $180^\circ$ about $I$ gives the triangle $A'B'C'$. The lines $AD, B'C'$ meet at $U$, the lines $BE, A'C'$ meet at $V$, and the lines $CF, A'B'$ meet at $W$. The line $BC$ meets $A'C', A'B'$ at $D_1, D_2$, respectively; the line $AC$ meets $A'B', B'C'$ at $E_1, E_2$, respectively; and the line $AB$ meets $B'C', A'C'$ at $F_1,F_2$, respectively. Six (not necessarily convex) quadrilaterals are colored orange: $$AUIF_2,\ C'FIF_2,\ BVID_1,\ A'DID_2,\ CWIE_1,\ B'EIE_2,$$ and six other quadrilaterals are colored green: $$AUIE_2,\ C'FIF_1,\ BVIF_2,\ A'DID_1,\ CWID_2,\ B'EIE_1.$$ Prove that the sum of the green areas equals the sum of the orange areas.

In a room there are several people; some of them always lie and all the others always tell the truth. Their ages are pairwise distinct. Each person says one of the following phrases:

"In this room there are as many truth-tellers older than me as liars younger than me", or

"In this room there are as many truth-tellers younger than me as liars older than me".

What is the maximum possible number of truth-tellers in the room? Find an example in which this maximum is achieved and prove that a larger number is impossible.

Nonzero real numbers $a,b,c,d,e,f,k,m$ satisfy $$\frac{a}{b}+\frac{c}{d}+\frac{e}{f}=k,\qquad \frac{b}{c}+\frac{d}{e}+\frac{f}{a}=m,\qquad ad=be=cf.$$ Express $\frac{a}{c}+\frac{c}{e}+\frac{e}{a}+\frac{b}{d}+\frac{d}{f}+\frac{f}{b}$ in terms of $m$ and $k$.

Let $w$ be a circle of diameter $5$. Four parallel lines divide $w$ into $5$ strips, each of width $1$. The strips are colored orange and purple alternately. Which area is larger: the orange or the purple?
Find all triples $(a,b,c)$ of integers for which the equation $$x^3-a^2x^2+b^2x-ab+3c=0$$ has three distinct integer roots $x_1,x_2,x_3$ which are pairwise coprime.

A convex paper quadrilateral $ABCD$ is called folding if there are points $P,Q,R,S$ in the interiors of the segments $AB,BC,CD,DA$, respectively, such that if we fold in the triangles $SAP$, $PBQ$, $QCR$, $RDS$, they exactly cover the quadrilateral $PQRS$; that is, the folded triangles cover $PQRS$ and do not overlap each other. Prove that if the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is folding, then $AC\perp BD$ or $ABCD$ is a trapezoid.
Let $x,y,z$ be non-negative real numbers. Prove that $$\sqrt{(2x+y)(2x+z)}+\sqrt{(2y+x)(2y+z)}+\sqrt{(2z+x)(2z+y)}\geq \sqrt{(x+2y)(x+2z)}+\sqrt{(y+2x)(y+2z)}+\sqrt{(z+2x)(z+2y)}.$$

Gandalf (the wizard) and Bilbo (the assistant) present a magic trick to Nitzan (the audience). While Gandalf is out of the room, Nitzan chooses a number $1\leq x\leq 2^{2022}$ and shows it to Bilbo. Bilbo then writes on the board a row of $N$ digits, each $0$ or $1$. After this Nitzan may, if he wishes, swap two consecutive digits of the row, but only once. Then Gandalf returns, looks at the row, and guesses the number $x$. Can Bilbo and Gandalf agree on a strategy which allows Gandalf to guess $x$ correctly no matter how Nitzan acts, if

(a) $N=2500$?

(b) $N=2030$?

(c) $N=2040$?
Solve the following system over the real numbers: $$\begin{cases}5x+5y+5xy-2xy^2-2x^2y=20,\\ 3x+3y+3xy+xy^2+x^2y=23.\end{cases}$$

A positive integer $x$ satisfies $$\left\{\frac{x}{3}\right\}+\left\{\frac{x}{5}\right\}+\left\{\frac{x}{7}\right\}+\left\{\frac{x}{11}\right\}=\frac{248}{165}.$$ Find all possible values of $$\left\{\frac{2x}{3}\right\}+\left\{\frac{2x}{5}\right\}+\left\{\frac{2x}{7}\right\}+\left\{\frac{2x}{11}\right\},$$ where $\{y\}$ denotes the fractional part of $y$.

A triangle is composed of circular cells arranged in $5784$ rows: the first row has one cell, the second has two cells, and so on, each cell touching its neighbors in its own row and in the adjacent rows. The cells are divided into pairs of adjacent cells (circles touching each other), so that each cell belongs to exactly one pair. A pair of adjacent cells is called diagonal if its two cells are not in the same row. What is the minimum possible number of diagonal pairs in such a division?

An acute triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle with center $O$. The reflections of $O$ in the three altitudes of the triangle are $U$, $V$, $W$: $U$ in the altitude from $A$, $V$ in the altitude from $B$, and $W$ in the altitude from $C$. Let $\ell_A$ be the line through $A$ parallel to $VW$, and define $\ell_B$, $\ell_C$ similarly. Prove that the lines $\ell_A$, $\ell_B$, $\ell_C$ are concurrent.

For an integer $k>1$, let $p(k)$ be its smallest prime divisor. Given an integer $a_1>2$, define an infinite sequence by $a_{n+1}=a_n^n-1$ for $n\geq 1$. For which values of $a_1$ is the sequence $p(a_n)$ bounded?

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle. Let $\omega_A$, $\omega_B$, $\omega_C$, $\omega_D$ be the incircles of the triangles $DAB$, $ABC$, $BCD$, $CDA$, respectively. The common external tangent of $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ different from the line $AB$ meets the common external tangent of $\omega_A$ and $\omega_D$ different from $AD$ at the point $A'$. Similarly, the common external tangent of $\omega_B$ and $\omega_C$ different from $BC$ meets the common external tangent of $\omega_C$ and $\omega_D$ different from $CD$ at $C'$. Prove that $AA'\parallel CC'$.

A rook stands on a cell of an infinite square grid. A different cell is colored blue, and mines are placed in $n$ other cells; the rook cannot stand on or pass through them. It is known that the rook can reach the blue cell in finitely many moves. Can it always do so (for every $n$ and every such choice of mines, starting cell and blue cell) in at most

(a) $1.99n+100$ moves?

(b) $2n-2\sqrt{3n}+100$ moves?

(In each move the rook moves along a row or a column.)

Let $n$ be a positive integer. $n$ letters are written around a circle, each of them $A$, $B$ or $C$. When the letters are read clockwise, the sequence $AB$ appears $100$ times, the sequence $BA$ appears $99$ times, and the sequence $BC$ appears $17$ times. How many times does the sequence $CB$ appear?

Let $ABCD$ be a rhombus. Eight further points $X_1$, $X_2$, $Y_1$, $Y_2$, $Z_1$, $Z_2$, $W_1$, $W_2$ are chosen so that the quadrilaterals $AX_1BX_2$, $BY_1CY_2$, $CZ_1DZ_2$, $DW_1AW_2$ are squares. Prove that the eight new points lie on two straight lines.

Bart wrote the digit $1$ $2024$ times in a row. Then Lisa wrote $2024$ more digits to the right of Bart's digits, such that the resulting number is the square of an integer. Find all possibilities for the digits Lisa wrote.

A $100\times \sqrt{3}$ rectangular table is given. What is the minimum number of disk-shaped napkins of radius $1$ needed to cover the table completely? (The napkins may overlap and may protrude beyond the edges of the table.)

$2024$ otters live in a river, and some of them are friends with each other. Is it possible that for any collection of $1012$ otters there is exactly one other otter that is friends with all $1012$ of them?
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be non-negative numbers such that $ab+ac+bc+abc=4$. Prove that $$\sqrt{\frac{ab+ac+1}{a+2}}+\sqrt{\frac{ab+bc+1}{b+2}}+\sqrt{\frac{ac+bc+1}{c+2}}\leq3.$$

For a positive integer $n$, let $A_n$ be the set of quadruples $(a,b,c,d)$ of integers satisfying simultaneously

• $0\le a\le c\le n$,

• $0\le b\le d\le n$,

• $c+d>n$, and

• $bc=ad+1$.

Define $$\alpha_n=\sum_{(a,b,c,d)\in A_n}\frac{1}{ab+cd}.$$ Find all real numbers $t$ such that $\alpha_n>t$ for every positive integer $n$.
